story: Russia has not had a competitive national election since the 1990s, but the Kremlin still holds them, carefully, because they are meant to show unity. In 2026, the first parliamentary election since Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine was designed to show a country united behind the war.

From 18 to 20 September, United Russia, Putin's party, won 349 of the 450 seats in the State Duma, more than three-quarters and the most any party has ever held (AP via National Herald). It took about 58 percent of the vote, up from under 50 percent in 2021. The only party opposed to the war, Yabloko, was barred from taking part by the Supreme Court, and no international observers from the OSCE were invited (Northeast Times). The new Duma includes 46 veterans of the war in Ukraine, a sign of how the Kremlin is building a new elite out of those who fought. Putin called the result a show of public support. The vote took place under constant Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian cities and refineries, as the war passed four and a half years and Russia's economy strained under a growing budget deficit. The EU's foreign policy chief called it another setback for Russian democracy.
briefing.power: Formally a federal presidential republic; in practice an authoritarian system centred on Putin. The president is head of state, commands the military and appoints the prime minister and government. The Duma, elected by a mixed system, approves laws the Kremlin sends it. Opposition parties and independent media have been banned or driven abroad.
briefing.holders: President Vladimir Putin, in power as president or prime minister since 1999; Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.
